title: The Fires on the Ground
author: Orrin Pale, sexton of Oakhaven
summary: The Oakhaven sexton's account of the winter after the Fracture, when the orchards blew away, the town starved, and the ground had to be burned before it could be dug.
text: I am not a writing man. I dig. But the Cantor says that what is written is kept, and somebody should keep this winter, and he has enough to carry, so I have taken it on. These are the dead of Oakhaven from the day the orchards went to the day the wagons came, and what it took to put them down.

The orchards went on a still morning at the back end of summer. I was in the churchyard turning the new plot for old Hesketh's widow, who was ailing, and I felt it before I heard it: a sort of hiss in the air, like milk boiling over on the far side of a wall. Then the wind came off the hills, and the reed-rows below the town, that had sung every wind of my life, did not sing. They chimed once, thin, like a glass knocked with a nail, and then the whole valley of them lifted off their stalks and went past me in a glitter. It got in my hair and my collar and my mouth. The children ran after it with their tongues out because it looked like sugar. It tasted of nothing at all. That frightened me more than the rest of it, and I could not have said why.
By evening there was not a standing reed in the Reach, and the Cantor was walking the rows with his hands open, the way you walk a field after hail.

The milk soured that night, every pail in the town. The dogs began howling at noon, which they had never done, and went on doing it all winter. When I tolled for Hesketh's widow in the first week of autumn, the bell came out flat. Not cracked. Flat, by a hair, as if it were somebody else's bell ringing in the next valley. Every person in the square stopped and looked up at the tower. I rang it out, because she was owed it, and then I tied off the rope. I have not tolled since. The Chapel-reader says it is the same everywhere, that the whole world has gone a little out of true and will come right with prayer. I pray. I have not untied the rope.

Then the grain from the south stopped. The carters said the roads were bad. The carters stopped coming to say it. The Governor stood on the Greenhall step and told us to keep faith and to ration, and we did both, and only one of them lasted.

The winter wheat came up wrong. It came up early and white and very fast, and stood in the field like a crop of straws, and when you split the ear there was nothing in it but a bead of water. Coker the miller ground what there was and wept at the stones, which I had not known a miller could do. By midwinter we had eaten the seed-corn. Everybody knew what that meant. Nobody said it.

Then the frost came. I have dug this ground forty years and never once met frost below the turf. The Reach does not freeze; everybody knows it. That winter it froze a spade's depth down and then two, hard as a step, and the spade rang off it and jarred me to the teeth. So I went to the woodpile.

This is the way I found to do it. The night before a burying I laid a fire on the grave's length, furze first and then whatever would burn, and sat up with it till the small hours, and raked it out and dug the soft hand's depth it had made, and laid another on top, and so on down. Three nights for a grown man. Two for a child. I will not write how many nights there were. I will write who they were for.
Wilf and Alban Wetherby, twins, four years old, the week before Candlefast, in one grave, because I had not the wood for two and their mother said they had never slept apart.

Essa Brindle, who went into the Flume at the sluice-gate. There was nothing to put in the ground. The Cantor sang her down at the gate, and I stood by with my spade because it did not seem right to come without it.
Tilda Hale, nine years.
Mother Peascod, who gave her bread to the Wetherby girl and did not tell anyone, and was found in her chair.

By Candlefast we were boiling harness. I want that written plainly, because people will say afterward it cannot have been so bad. It was the Governor's own carriage-harness first. He sent it down to the Greenhall kitchen himself and stood at the copper while it boiled, so that nobody could say he had kept it back.

Lettie, Osgood and the baby, the miller's three, in the space of nine days. Lambert Coker dug alongside me for the last of them and would not be stopped, and the two of us sat by the fire on his daughter's grave all night, and he told me every word she had ever learned, in order, which I think is the longest anybody has ever spoken to me.
Jonas Garlick, who walked out into the dead reed-rows one night and lay down in the dust, and was found smiling.

Hobday's infant, three days old. Bettany the midwife brought her to me herself, wrapped, and said that was the seventh child I had had off her that winter and she would bring me no more if she could help it, and then she sat down on my step and could not get up for a while.
The Sawtell brothers, both together, of the cold, in the cart-shed where they had gone to save the walk home.

Widow Dimmock. Old Hesketh's sister. Two of the Ackroyd household, whose names their mother has asked me to leave out, and I have. A carter from Greenroot whose name nobody knew, who came up the road with an empty cart to ask if we had anything, and stayed.

That is seventeen, and Hesketh's widow before them, who would have gone in any year. The Cantor sang every one of them. Some nights he sang with nothing left in him but breath, and I could hear his breath going down into the ground with them, and it was enough. He says a song for the dead does not have to be heard by the living. I hope that is true. There were not many living out by then.

In the spring the frost went out of the ground all at once, in a night, and the next morning forty wagons came up the Greenroot road with grain under the sheets and men in green and black walking beside them. The Governor went out to meet them in the square in his good coat. There was a paper. He read it at the table in the Greenhall with the doors open and the whole town standing in the square outside, smelling the sacks, and nobody inside or out said a word. Then he signed it.

I do not know what was in it. I have heard it said since that he sold something that was not his to sell. I will say this, and then I will stop. I am the one man in Oakhaven who knows to the night what it cost not to sign. I have put the spade back on its pegs, and I have let the fires go out, and I do not mean to be the one who tells him he paid too much.
notes: Sources: Book One ch. 1 (the wind-reeds turning to spun sugar and blowing to dust on the day the Spire broke; Cantors sing the dead into the ground; the Chapel's peal of six and the town clock-bell, later taken for bore-teeth "in the first year of the quarry", so they are still hanging here); ch. 2 (Aldric: the orchards went in an hour, the wheat came up wrong, the seed-corn eaten by midwinter, harness leather by Candlefast, the Wetherby twins, the Hale girl, the miller's three and eleven more buried, fires burned on the ground to get the spade in, forty wagons of grain and a paper up the Greenroot road in spring); Series Bible Part IV "The World Went Flat" (milk souring overnight, dogs howling at noon, a quarter-tone wrong); Tobin's Journal p. 3 (Phase 6: grain from the south stopped; "We are told the Cascade was nobody's fault. The Governor says to keep faith and ration"); Bettany the midwife (Series Bible Part VIII). Deliberately absent: hounds in Oakhaven (Tobin p. 10 has the first hounds at the orchards in 417), hush-lamps and night-hummers (Tam is a night-hummer "since the first autumn of the Hedge"), stones on the tongue (ch. 1 has the sexton start that custom only when the graves began to heave), and Kaelen's homecoming (its season is unclear between ch. 1 and ch. 2). Canon tension noted: Vol V calls 419 the Reach's first winter in living memory, but ch. 2's frozen ground stands, so the sexton treats 412 as the one frost he ever met below the turf. [PROPOSED]: Orrin Pale (the Chapel sexton of Phase 16) as sexton already in 412 and as this book's author; the first names Wilf and Alban Wetherby, Tilda Hale, the miller Lambert Coker and his children, and the other dead named here (Essa Brindle, Mother Peascod, Jonas Garlick, Hobday's infant, the Sawtell brothers, Widow Dimmock); the custom of the sexton tolling the town bell for the dead; the reed-dust tasting of nothing.

title: The Wool Wall
author: Dorcas Ribble, carder at the Carders' mill
summary: The carder who first proposed the Hedge tells how Oakhaven planted it in one season, out of thorn and the fleece of every sheep in the Reach.
text: It was my idea. I want that written down in my own hand, while there is still time to be blamed for it properly.

The hounds came at the turn of the year. Not into the town. They came to the edge of the orchards on a Massday night and sat down in a row in the dust where the reeds used to be, eleven of them, with their heads on one side, like a congregation waiting for the reader. They did not howl. They listened. In the morning they were gone, and every one of us had lain awake till dawn trying to remember whether we had made a sound.

The Cantor sent to the three nearest parishes for help. Two Cantors came. The third sent a note that said: We have stopped being able to send. They sat in the Greenhall all one afternoon with the Governor and the bench, and talked about walls and fires and singing, and every plan was a loud one, because men's plans are. I was there to bring the bread. I am not on the bench and never wished to be.

I said, it isn't a wall you want. It's a stopper. You pad a cradle against a draught. Pad the town. Wool eats sound; I have stood in the fleece-loft at the mill with forty bales round me and heard my own heart. Plant thorn deep, so nothing can come through it, and pack the thorn with wool, so nothing can hear through it.
Nobody laughed, which was worse than if they had. The Cantor wrote yes in his register, and looked at it, and said he did not feel any better, and nor did I.

He did not see it go in. The hounds had him at the Pellow farm in the spring, and the Hedge went in that summer without him. The Consortium paid. I set that down too, since it is the one time. They sent wagons of blackthorn and hawthorn whips from somewhere south, and bramble crowns in wet sacking, and a young engineer in green and black with a bag of pegs and a measuring chain, who walked the line of it round the town in two days and stuck a peg every ten paces and never once asked anybody what the Hedge was for. He knew. He had the kind face of a man who has been told not to look up from his chain.

The wool was ours. Every sheep in the Reach came to be shorn. The Farrants brought the Downs flocks down off the sheep-walk in one great grey river, and the Wethercombe folk came in behind them with their carts and their bedding, and the Bellwether put up its shutters, and the fold on the Downs was left standing empty with the gate open. We shore in the square, in the lanes, in the Chapel porch. We shore ewes that had been shorn in spring and had barely a fleece to give. The mill book says nine thousand fleeces by the end, and that is not counting what came in loose in sacks from the far farms, smelling of the hill.

We carded it all. That was our part. The mill engine ran day and night until it was too hot to stand by, and then we carded by hand on our knees in the yard, all of us, the old women and the girls and the men who had never touched a card in their lives, by lamp, in our aprons, with our hands bleeding into the fleece. Nell sang the work-song all night, the whole of it and then from the top again, and nobody asked her to be quiet, because it was the last night anybody would have to ask.

This is how it went in. Thorn in a trench as deep as a man's waist. A man's height of packed wool either side of it, rammed down with posts. Thorn again. Wool again. Felt and old sacking hung over the top, straw in the roots, three men deep all the way round. Four hundred hands, and the Governor's two, which blistered on the first morning and which he would not have bound. He worked the north side with the carters and did not speak to anybody, and was there at dusk and there at dawn.

When the last row went in at the North Gate, somebody said we should try it. So the whole town stood on the rise inside the thorn and shouted together, every one of us, as loud as we could, the first loud sound any of us had made since the hounds came. It went into the Hedge like a stone into a pond with no bottom. No echo. Not a whisper of one. It was the most terrible thing I have ever heard, and we cheered it, and then we stood there and were very quiet, because we could be.
Harrow has the gate key now. The gate shuts at dusk.

I go round the Hedge most evenings, along the inside, looking for where the wool has slipped. It has grown a yard since we planted it, the thorn. Everything grows here now, faster than it ought. The flocks are inside with us, in the paddocks behind the tannery and the orchard closes and anywhere there is grass, and one of the Farrants walks them every morning and counts them every night. There are a great many sheep and a great many of us, and the winter is coming, and I have not yet heard anyone say aloud what everyone has worked out. I will not say it either.
I said a stopper. I did not stop to think what a stopper does with what it stops. A cork does not throw the wine away. It keeps it.

I know wool. I have handled it all my life. Wool keeps. It keeps the warmth of the one who wore it, and the shape of them, long after they have taken it off; you can lift a shawl off a peg a week after a woman has gone and still find her shoulders in it. Every sound this town makes goes into my wool now and does not come out the other side. That was the whole of the plan, and it works, and I am proud of it, and on still nights I put my hand flat on the fleece at the cooperage wall, the way a person feels a loaf to see whether it has proved, and it is warm.
notes: Sources: Book One ch. 1 (blackthorn, bramble and hawthorn three men deep; packed with wool by the cartload, felt and sacking hung, straw in the roots; the Consortium paid for the planting and the town did the rest; every small sound goes in and does not come out; the gate of oak and iron); Tobin's Journal pp. 10 and 11 (Phase 6: the first hounds sitting at the orchard edge, eleven in a row, high summer 417; the Cantors of three parishes called, "We have stopped being able to send"; "It was a carder from the mill who said it... a stopper"; four hundred hands and the Governor's two, which blistered; thorn in the trench, a man's height of wool either side; the carders in aprons all night by lamp; Nell sang the work-song until morning; the whole town calling out together and no echo; the gate shut at dusk, Harrow keeps the key); Book Four Part One (planted autumn 417; raw wool from every sheep in the Reach; "the Synod's engineers"); Phase 20-21 Author Rulings (the Downs flocks driven down to be shorn and kept inside the Hedge, where over the shut years they were eaten; nothing took them); Phase 22 (Wethercombe folk went in; the Bellwether shut the night the Hedge closed; the Farrants' sheep-walk). The author does not yet know the flocks will be eaten, only fears it. Tobin is not named, and his fate is not dated, because ch. 1 and the journal disagree on the season. [PROPOSED]: Dorcas Ribble as the unnamed carder of Tobin's page 10 and as author; the Consortium engineer with pegs and a chain who laid out the line (reconciling "the town did the rest" with Book Four's "the Synod's engineers"); the dye-vats; the wool counted by the fleece in the mill book; the yard of growth since the planting. Owner ruling (Oct 2026): the manuscript wins. The hounds reach the orchards at the turn of 417, Tobin is taken in the spring at the Pellow farm, and the Hedge goes in that summer, paid for by the Consortium.

title: What Came Up the Greenroot Road
author: Josiah Seddon, under-clerk at the Greenhall
summary: A Greenhall under-clerk sets down, very carefully, how the Consortium of Bores came to Oakhaven between the famine spring of 413 and the bore, and what he copied along the way.
text: I have been under-clerk at the Greenhall for eleven years. I copy what I am given and I file what I copy, and I have never once been asked what I think of it, which suits me. What follows is not what I think. It is only the order things happened in, which is a clerk's business, and which I find is already being forgotten.

Spring, 413. The forty wagons came up the Greenroot road the week the frost went out of the ground. I counted them from the Greenhall step because counting is what I do when I am frightened. Forty, each with a sheet roped over it and a man in green and black walking at the wheel. They stopped in the square and nobody unroped a single sheet. They did not need to. The whole town could smell the grain.

The paper was two sides long. I held the wax. The heading was the Consortium of Bores, and the body was grain against survey: so many wagons now and so many to follow, in return for the right to measure the quarry and the ground beneath it, and first refusal of whatever the measuring found. The Governor read it through twice at the table with the doors open and the square full of people outside, not one of them speaking. Then he said, "Write that the Governor signs for bread," and I wrote it in the margin of the minute, and he signed. His hand is large, and it shook, and the S of his name goes through two lines. I made the fair copy myself. I have it still.

Frostmonth, 413. The surveyors came. Three of them, in grey, with brass staves and a measuring chain, walking the Flume bank by the Carders' mill one pace at a time and writing every pace down. They drove a stake above the sluice and hung a little glass bell on it, and the bell hummed by itself, very low. The Cantor put his hand on the post and said it was our note, coming up out of the ground. I minuted the visit as Survey, Consortium, one day, no charge.

Harvestmonth, 414. The lease. I want to set the words down exactly, because people say them wrong. The Consortium of Bores takes the quarry, the shaft, and such resonances as lie beneath. In return, bread: a cart a week, at a fixed price, for nine years. The Governor read it aloud standing, in his good coat, and did not look at the room. The bench voted. One voice against, and it was the Cantor's, and I wrote it down: Ashgrove, no. Then I wrote the rest, ayes, carried. I have looked at that page a good deal since. It is the neatest page in the book.

415 and 416. The works. You will know them. The fence round the headframe, that hums if you lay a hand on it. The sheds, the stores, the pay-office where the men are paid in the Consortium's paper, which the Consortium's stores take and nobody else's do. The mast, a hundred and twenty feet of riveted iron on four legs bolted into the quarry rim, that took a summer to raise and that every child in the Reach climbed the hill to look at. A Factor came to live in the works house, in black with green at the cuffs. Grain came every week, as the lease said. Nobody went hungry. I want that set down, because it is true.

417. The bore. They began to sink it and the ground began to ache. You felt it in your teeth before you heard it, a grinding a long way down that has not stopped since. The bells went that year: the Chapel's six and the clock-bell off the Greenhall roof and the little bells in the old reed-rows. A young man of the Church came with the Consortium's cart and said it was a blessing, and the bronze went down the quarry road to be made into teeth for the bore. I minuted it as Requisition, bronze, by order, no charge. That is the second time I have written no charge on a thing that cost us a great deal.

The tankers began after that, once a day, east toward the Organum, green glass sloshing behind iron grilles, and a soldier with a bell for a head walking on either side. The oaks began to ring when the wind moved them. A notice came saying no oak was to be felled, the oaks being now the property of the Consortium, like the quarry, and the Root, and the glass. I had not known until I copied that notice that the Root was a thing that could be owned. I had not known it was a thing at all.

Then we lost the Cantor, and the week after, two men in green and black came to the Greenhall with a crate, and carried his chair out from the Governor's right hand, and put the Queen's seal up in its place: pale green glass, a yard across, with her face pressed into it. I was told to see it dusted.
That is the order things happened in. Here is the one thing I have noticed, and then I will put this away.

Every decree that comes to the Greenhall now comes BY ROYAL ASSENT, under Queen Maelis's seal and signature. I have copied some hundreds of them. I have them in the press beside my desk, and in the same press, at the bottom, I have my fair copy of the paper of 413. When nobody is in the hall I sometimes lay them side by side.

The Queen's hand is small and beautiful and it does not shake. It has not shaken once in a hundred and some decrees. People in the square say that is because she is a hundred and forty years dead, and they say it very quietly, and I do not repeat it.
The Governor's hand goes through two lines.
I am a clerk. I am not supposed to have an opinion about signatures. But I know which of those two hands was afraid of what it was signing, and I know which one I would rather trust.
notes: Sources: Book One ch. 2 (Aldric: forty wagons of grain and a paper up the Greenroot road in the spring after the Fracture, "And I signed it"; the Greenhall's carvings hung with Synod and Consortium banners, the Queen's glass seal a yard across where the Cantor's chair used to stand; Tobin in the Cantor's chair on court days; Consortium scrip; the Resident Factor); ch. 1 (bells requisitioned "in the first year of the quarry" because the bore's teeth needed bronze; tanker-wagons east toward the Organum with a Legionnaire either side; the oaks ringing since the bore; felling forbidden because the oaks are Consortium property like the quarry, the Root and the glass; decrees "BY ROYAL ASSENT" over Queen Maelis's seal, her signature very steady, dead a hundred and forty years); ch. 12 (the mooring mast, a hundred and twenty feet of riveted iron on four splayed legs in the bedrock of the quarry rim); Tobin's Journal pp. 4, 5 and 9 (Phase 6: surveyors in grey with brass staves and a chain on the Flume bank by the Carders' mill in Frostmonth 413, a small glass bell on a stake humming the Root's note; the lease read aloud in Harvestmonth 414, the quarry, the shaft and "such resonances as lie beneath" for a cart of bread a week at a fixed price for nine years, the Cantor the only vote against; the fenced headframe that hums; the bore begun in 417). Reconciliation: the 413 paper (ch. 2) is treated as a grain agreement giving survey rights, and the 414 lease (Tobin) as the lease proper, so both stand. The bells are dated to the first year of the bore, following the manuscript over Tobin's p. 3. Tobin's taking is mentioned without a season. [PROPOSED]: Josiah Seddon and his office; the clerk's habit of keeping copies in a press; the wording "grain against survey"; the words quoted from the 413 paper.

title: Tench's Reach Almanack for the Year 419
author: Cuthbert Tench, almanack-maker; with notes in the margin by Ezra Dunnock, farmer
origin: printed at Stillwater Landing; annotated in Oakhaven
summary: A cheap printed almanack of feasts, weather and planting for the Reach in 419, argued with all year in the margins by an Oakhaven farmer.
text: TENCH'S REACH ALMANACK for the Year 419. Feasts, Weather, Planting and Sundry Useful Matters, for the Use of Households in the Reach and along the Flume. Printed at Stillwater Landing. One Chime, or the value.
In the margin: Paid a Chime for it at the gate. A Chime! Ezra Dunnock, his book, north field, Oakhaven.

THE COMPILER TO HIS READERS. The year has three hundred and sixty days, twelve months of thirty and forty-five weeks of eight, and so every date falls on the same day of the week as it did last year and will next. A household that keeps this almanack need never buy another. The compiler hopes it will.
In the margin: He hopes it will not, or he is a poor sort of tradesman.

THE EIGHT DAYS, and their old uses, as the country people keep them. Rootday, for setting and sowing. Hearthday, for baking. Massday, for carting and heavy work. Stasisday, for mending what is broken. Dawnday, for the Chapel. Driftday, for journeys. Memoryday, for letters to the absent. Nullday, for rest.

In the margin: My gran would not fell a tree on a Rootday. Said that was the trees' own day and you let them have it. Nobody rests on Nullday. You keep somebody by you on Nullday and you leave the lamp in.

STILLMONTH. The year begins on the first, which is a Dawnday, as it always is, the morning after the Longest Night. The Hearth Feast, the lighting of the forges, on Hearthday the sixth: chiefly kept in the Caldera. Weather: open and mild, as is usual in the Reach. Mend tools, prune, carry muck.
In the margin: Mild. Mended the long fence. Nobody here has lit a forge for a feast in my life.

THAWMONTH. Ice off the Flume, where there is any. Contract Day, the Feast of the Dial, on Stasisday the second, when every term in the province falls due and is made again. Settle accounts. Turn the soil when it will take the spade.

In the margin: There's no ice on the Flume. There never is. Tench has copied that out of somebody's book from the Peaks. Contract Day: went to the Greenhall to make my ground-rent again. The clerk wrote the same figure. Nobody makes a term again in Oakhaven. They copy it out.

SEEDMONTH. The Root Feast on Rootday the first: the planting feast, the one day of the year kept loud on purpose. Sow barley, oats and beans. This is the loudest month in the Reach and the compiler wishes his readers a noisy one.

In the margin: We were loud. Inside the wool, all of us in the square, the old planting song, the whole of it, top to bottom, the first time since the Hedge. The Hedge took it. Nothing came. Then everyone went home very quick and quiet as if we'd done something wrong. Sowed the north field Rootday. The ground said wait. I didn't.
LAMBMONTH. Lambing. Weather: soft. Sow the late peas. Watch the hedges for nesting.
In the margin: No lambs. The flocks went into the Hedge two years back and into us after. Watched the Hedge anyway. It nests something. Not birds.
REEDMONTH. When the wind-reeds come up, Reed-Hanging: take down last year's reeds over the door and hang new, cut to each child's own note. The Cantor's year properly begins.

In the margin: No wind-reeds since the year the Spire went. Cut the girl's new reed from the beds by the Flume, same as last year, and the Cantor tuned it at the door against her own breastbone, and it hangs there. Flume reed does well enough. It doesn't sing like the old ones. Nothing does.
LONGSUN. Hay. The Empyrean, the dawn service, on Dawnday the third, which all are bound to attend. The Longest Day on the thirtieth, a Nullday, on which there is no feast and nothing is to be done.

In the margin: Stood in the square at dawn as the paper says. Chapel-reader read the service. Nobody sang. Did nothing on the thirtieth. Felt it all day, like weather coming. Hay was in twice. Cut it Massday and it stood again by Dawnday, thinner. The second hay smells of nothing.
DUSTMONTH. Dry. The Feast of the Drift and the Great Race on Driftday the sixth, on the Coast, where the captains keep it. Water stock. Watch for fire.

In the margin: Not dry. Damp all month, and everything growing as if it were being chased. Sapling up through the yard cobbles. Sawed it. It came back from the cut by morning. Sawed it again. That is my Dustmonth, Tench.
FIRSTFRUIT. Early apples, plums. The Eel-Run, the night the eels go down the Flume, late in the month: lanterns, traps, and quiet.
In the margin: No eels. Old men at the crossing say they'll go down late and they've never been wrong about eels. Apples split on the bough from swelling. Pressed what I could.
SHEAFMONTH. Reaping. The Keystone, the Weighing at Fortis, on Massday the seventh, where the soldiers weigh their kit and cut names in the wall. Bind sheaves dry.

In the margin: Harrow had it off a carter that they cut more names this year than last at Fortis. Reaped the long field. Bread from it tastes of the bin. Third cut since the spring. Every cut is less. My girl asked why bread used to taste of something. I said it still does, you're just used to it. She knew I was lying. They always do, at eight.

HARVESTMONTH. The Last Sheaf, which the almanack cannot date, for it falls when the last field is cut, and is known by the sheaf hung on the gate. The whole village cuts the last stand together, one cut to the beat. The sheaf is plaited and hung over the gate till spring, and is the one sheaf the Reach lets stay cut.

In the margin: The last stand is mine this year, in the north field, the corner by the oaks. Had the plait-straw ready and the girl had her ribbon. Then the Church came up the Greenroot road singing their one note with the white fire on poles, and the reader read it out in the square: there is to be a Rite on Hearthday the sixteenth, and the Last Sheaf is to wait until after, so as not to sing two things at once. So it waits. It stands there in the corner with the light on it. I went out at dusk and put my hand on it. Feels like it's waiting for something.
ASHFALL. Lift roots. The Canopy, the remembering of the dead, on Memoryday the seventh. (Not presently kept.)

FROSTMONTH. Mild, as is usual in the Reach. Ringing-Wood Day at the first hard frost, when the year's timber is felled and named. The Longest Night on the thirtieth, a Stasisday. The Reach has known one hard winter in living memory, in the year of the Fracture, and the almanack does not look for another.
In the margin, the last thing written in the book: Sheaf still standing. We'll cut it when we're let.

The margins end before Ashfall, so the Leaf-Fall and the winter of 419 are not foreseen. title: The Orchard Craft: A Short History of the Cantors of the Reach
author: Jessamy Yarrow, Cantor, of the Reedside Conservatory
summary: Written while the wind-reed orchards still sang, a Cantor's proud, funny and slightly cross account of what her craft is, where it came from, and why it is not a church.
text: I have been asked by the Cantor-Master to write down the history of our craft for the new students, because the Conservatory has a library and the library has a gap on its shelf where our history ought to be. I said that the craft has no history, only a great many old women who remember things. She said, then write down the old women. So I have.

Nobody knows how old the craft is. Ask a Cantor and she will hum at you, which is not an answer but is the truth. It is older than the Greenhall, which the Cantors built three hundred years ago as a guildhall for the reed-growers, and where a Cantor still sits at the Governor's right hand on court days and hums when the petitions grow dull. It is older than the reed-orchards. My own teacher, Mother Sefton, who was ninety when she taught me and had been taught by a woman of ninety, used to say that the craft was old when the Synod was a rumour, and that it would be old when the Synod was a rumour again. She said this in the Chapel porch, loudly. She was a great trial to the Chapel-reader.

What is the craft? People from outside the Reach think it is singing. It is not, or not chiefly. It is listening, and then giving back the right note at the right moment, and very often the right note is barely a note at all.

A student comes to the Conservatory at eight, and the first thing she learns is not a song but a breath: four counts in, a long fall out. For a year she breathes on seedlings. Trees hear breath before voice. Children who come wanting to sing find this very dull, and the best of them go on finding it dull for about a month and then stop finding it anything, and that is how you know.

Then she learns the Root note, the note the whole Reach is tuned to: one hundred and seventy-four beats to the second, sung a hand's width above the ground with the mouth nearly closed. That is the note for bringing things on: seedlings, grafts, wounds, babies. A Cantor at a lying-in hums it into a clay jar pressed to the mother's belly, so that the note goes into the body instead of into the room. That trick is older than anything else we have, and it works, and nobody knows why, and every midwife in the Reach has learned it from one of us and pretends she thought of it herself. We let her.

Then she learns the falling fifth, which is the Root note and the note a fifth below it, for letting things down: a fever, a fright, a branch that has grown wrong. And the calling-song, the one loud thing in the craft, for bringing lost lambs home across three fields, which every student practises on the Conservatory roof at dusk and which the whole of Reedside has learned to sleep through. At sixteen, last of all, she learns the felling-song, which is sung to an old tree before the axe: the falling fifth held, let go, and then a note below it that you feel in the floor more than hear. It tells the sap to go down. I have sung it four times in my life and I wept at three of them, and so does everybody, and that is correct.

That is the whole of it. A breath, a note, a fifth, a call, a farewell. Everything else a Cantor does is made of those five things, put together in the right order for the person or the tree in front of her.

We have no catechism. I want that understood, because the Chapel-reader has more than once called the craft a superstition and more than once called it a heresy, and it cannot be both. We do not pray to the trees. We ask them things. A Cantor can lay her palm flat on the bark of an old pear and be still, and the tree will answer one question, yes or no, if you ask it plainly. That is not worship. That is manners.

The Church teaches that holiness is one note held without end, and that the second note is sin. I do not quarrel with the Church; it has its own business. But I will point out, for the students, that there is not one tending in the whole craft that is done on a single note. The fifth is two notes. The felling-song is three. The craft is made out of the distances between notes, the way a hedge is made out of the gaps between the stakes, and anyone who has stood in the orchards in a west wind knows that one note on its own is not a song. It is only a noise that has not been answered yet.

The orchards. The Cantors planted the wind-reed orchards row by row over three hundred years, and tuned them by pruning: you cut the long cane to sound the Root, and you let the others down a little at a time over many seasons, until a whole slope of them gives a chord when the wind comes off the hills. People in Greenroot, three miles off, know the weather by which chord the orchards are singing. There are rows on the south slope that were tuned by women whose names nobody remembers, and they are still in tune. That is our history. It is standing in the field.
Two customs I cannot explain, and will set down so that somebody else may.

First: there is a lullaby, five notes, a turn, the five again lower, and a fall, that every mother in the Reach sings, and every Cantor learns before any other song. It is the oldest thing we have. No one has ever said who made it or what it was first made for. Mother Sefton said it was made for something very large that could not sleep.

Second: on the Longest Night, every Cantor in the Reach goes out to the oldest tree in her orchard and hums into its hollow until dawn. I have done it every year of my life, with frost on my shawl, and I have never once been told why. When I asked Mother Sefton, she said only that it was done in place of. I said, in place of what? And she looked at me for a long time and said, in place of what we used to do, and would not say more, and I do not think she knew.

Every mending borrows. That is the last thing a student is told, and the first thing she forgets. A Cantor's voice is her own body, and whatever she gives out through it comes out of the same account. There are old Cantors in the Reach with no voice left at all, and they are not sorry.

I have written this down not because I am afraid our craft will be lost. Nothing the whole Reach hums in its sleep can be lost. I have written it so that the students have something on the shelf to argue with. If you want to know what this book was trying to say, put it down and go and stand in the reed-rows when the wind comes off the hills. They will tell you better than I can.
notes: Suggested library: the Conservatory. Sources: Series Bible Part III "the lost curriculum" (the Cantors' tending notes for births, fevers and apple trees) and Part VI (wind-reed orchards where Cantors trained; births hummed through clay jars); Vol III A.1 (the Cantor craft as the "old faith": practical, agricultural, un-theological); Book One ch. 1 (the clay jar as a trick older than the Synod; the Root note, 174; the falling fifth; the calling-song for bringing lost lambs home, loud; "Every mending borrows"; the wind-reeds planted in rows by the Cantors over three hundred years and tuned by pruning, heard from Greenroot; "Apples in the Rain"); ch. 2 (the Greenhall built three hundred years ago by the orchard-cantors as a guildhall for the reed-growers; the Cantor's chair at the Governor's right hand); ch. 9 (a five-note Cantor's lullaby); Vol V §4 (the tending breath at eight; "trees hear breath before voice"; the felling-song at sixteen, a falling fifth and the fall below the fall; asking a tree with the flat palm; humming into the hollow of the oldest orchard tree on the Longest Night as a remnant; Ilse Brennan Cantor-Master of the Reedside Conservatory for forty years, so in office in 396); Vol I §4.1 and §4.3 (the First Reed hung over the door at birth, pitched to the child's Signature; the Last Note held by the family); Vol I §4.2 (Synod schools correct children for singing); Series Bible Part III (the catechism: the second note is sin). The Cantors' Secret (Vol V §4) is only brushed: the author's teacher says the Longest Night humming is done "in place of" something, and does not say what. Written before 412, so the author expects the orchards to last. title: A First History of Oakhaven, for the Orchard School
author: Garra Thorne, teacher at the orchard school
summary: A schoolteacher's history of Oakhaven in eight short lessons, from three rival stories of its founding to the planting of the Hedge, with questions for her pupils at the end of each.
text: To the children of the orchard school. This book is to be read aloud in class, quietly, a lesson at a time. When you come to the questions, answer them on your slates. Do not shout out. You know why.

Lesson One. Where Oakhaven stands. Oakhaven is the chief town of the Resonant Reach. It stands on a rise above the Chlorophyll Flume, which is the green river that runs in a channel of grown wood and climbs when it should fall. Downriver, three miles east, is Greenroot. West are the Watch Downs and the combe at Wethercombe. East, a long way east, past the Spectral Woods, is the Organum, which you will not see, and need not. All round us are the iron-oaks, which ring when the wind moves them.
Questions. Which way does the Flume run? Which way does it want to run? Why do we not climb the oaks any more?
Lesson Two. How Oakhaven began. Nobody knows, and so there are three stories, and you may choose.

The drovers' story is that a man was bringing sheep down off the Downs in a storm, and lay down under the great oak on the green, the one we call the Old Haven, and the oak hummed him to sleep, and in the morning he would not leave, and built a house against its roots. That is why it is Oakhaven: a haven in the oaks.
The Cantors' story is that there were Cantors here before there were houses, singing to the orchards, and the town grew up round their school the way a village grows round a well.
The clerks' story is that Oakhaven began when somebody first wrote it down, and the first roll in the Greenhall is three hundred years old, so Oakhaven is three hundred years old.
The clerks' story is the only one with paper in it. It is also the only one nobody believes.
Questions. Which story do you like best? Which story do you think is true? Are those the same story?

Lesson Three. The Queens. Long ago the Reach had its own crown, as every one of the eight realms did. The last of our queens was Queen Maelis. Her face is on the green glass seal in the Greenhall and on every notice at the well-house. She reigns still, at the Organum, among the other monarchs of the Glass Court, and signs the Synod's decrees for us in her own hand.
We do not say more than that in school.
Questions. Copy out the words at the top of the newest notice on the well-house. Whose seal is under them?

Lesson Four. The Greenhall and the orchards. Three hundred years ago the Cantors built the Greenhall for the reed-growers, and carved every beam with reeds and apple boughs and singing birds. Over the same three hundred years they planted the wind-reed orchards below the town, row by row, and tuned them by pruning, so that when the wind came off the hills the whole valley sang. Your grandparents could tell you the weather by which chord the orchards were singing. Ask them.
Questions. Ask someone at home what the orchards sounded like. Write down what they say. If they will not say, write that down instead.

Lesson Five. The year the Spire broke. In 412, far away in the Dawning Heights, the great Spire of Light broke, and the whole world went a little out of tune. On the same morning every wind-reed in the Reach turned to something like glass and blew away as dust. The winter after was the hard winter, the only one anyone remembers, and seventeen people of Oakhaven died of it. The sexton has written an account. In the spring the Consortium of Bores brought grain up the Greenroot road, and the Governor signed for it, and Oakhaven ate.
Questions. Why do you think the Governor signed? What would you have done? (You may leave this one blank.)

Lesson Six. The quarry. In 414 the Consortium leased the quarry north of the town, and the shaft, and what was under it. They built the works, and the fence that hums, and the great iron mast. In 417 they began the bore. The bells of Oakhaven were taken down that year, all of them, and sent to the quarry. That is why there are no bells, and why, if you find a bell, you do not ring it.
Questions. Put your hand flat on the schoolroom floor. What do you feel? Do not write it down. Just know it.

Lesson Seven. The Hedge. In the summer of 417 the town planted the Hedge: blackthorn, bramble and hawthorn, three men deep, packed with the wool of every sheep in the Reach. Everybody helped. Some of you helped, though you were very small, carrying fleece in your aprons. The Hedge swallows every sound we make, so that nothing outside can hear us. That is why we are safe. That is why we murmur. That is why, when you are sent to the gate, you go no further than the gate.
Questions. Name the three trees of the Hedge. What is the wool for? Who keeps the key?

Lesson Eight. The last lesson. When you are grown, someone from outside may ask you what Oakhaven was. You will tell them about the oaks and the orchards and the Greenhall and the Hedge. I hope you will also tell them that the children of Oakhaven learned to murmur before they learned to read, and learned to read anyway, and that this was not nothing.
And one question, as always, to finish.
What is on the other side of the Hedge?
Do not answer this one aloud. Write it on your slate, and look at it, and then rub it out.
notes: Suggested library: the Conservatory. Sources: Vol V §4 "Other Reach Figures" (Garra Thorne, orchard-school teacher); Series Bible Part VI (Oakhaven capital of the Reach, Greenroot downriver, iron-oaks, the Chlorophyll Flume; Queen Maelis dead a hundred and forty years, her signature on Synod decrees), Part V (the Long Octave of eight crowned realms; the Glass Coronation c. 120 SR) and Part VIII (the Glass Court: nine revived monarchs who sign whatever is placed before them); Book One ch. 1 and 2 (the Greenhall built three hundred years ago by the Cantors; the orchards planted over three hundred years and blown to dust on the day the Spire broke; bells taken in the first year of the quarry; the Hedge of blackthorn, bramble and hawthorn; children learn to murmur before they read; "Does it ring?"); ch. 2 (the hard winter and the forty wagons); Tobin's Journal pp. 5 and 11 (Phase 6: the lease of 414; the planting of the Hedge, 417); Phase 22 (Wethercombe) and Phase 20 rulings (the Watch Downs west of Oakhaven); Series Bible (the mimic rule, never answer a voice you cannot see). Garra Thorne is later one of the twenty-five who said no in the Grove (Vol V); nothing here touches that. Written in spring 419, before the Rite. [PROPOSED]: Garra Thorne as the author of this schoolbook; the three founding stories (the drover under the humming oak, the Cantors' school, the clerks' rolls); the iron-oak called the Old Haven on the green; the school's slate custom of writing and rubbing out. Owner ruling (Oct 2026): the Hedge was planted "two summers ago" (manuscript), so the summer of 417.

title: Four Seconds at the Margin
author: Gerda Stahl, of Tier Three, Cinderhold; taken down and printed on Broadsheet Row
origin: printed on Broadsheet Row, Port Cantabile; carried up the river through Stillwater Landing
summary: A drill-hand of Cinderhold's Tier Three tells, between the hammer-falls, how nine hundred of her tier died in four seconds at the Thermal Margin, and why she is the one left to tell it.
text: Printed on Broadsheet Row. The printer's note: This was spoken to us by a woman of Cinderhold who came down the coast in the spring with nothing but a gauge-house key on a string. She would only talk between the falls of a hammer, so we found her one at the forge on the Lantern Yard, and wrote down what she said in the spaces. We have kept the spaces.
I am Gerda Stahl, of Tier Three. Still standing.
You want the Margin. Everyone wants the Margin. Let the hammer come round.

The Margin is the ring of drills outside the caldera, where the heat comes up out of the ground and the Consortium puts pipes in it. Tier Three works it. Worked it. Nine hundred and seven on the day shift, though nobody had counted until after. My Odo had the number-six head. I had the gauge-house behind it. That is a stone hut the size of a cart with a basalt wall a yard thick on the drill side, and a slot to read the needle through.

The order came on a Massday in 417, by a runner in grey. Pressure up by a third. The Synod wanted more out of the ground and wanted it before the Weighing. Our foreman read it out between falls. He said it was against the seal-tolerance. The runner said the tolerance had been revised. The foreman said, revised by who. The runner said, by people who are not standing here. That was true.
We put the pressure up. You do what the paper says. Odo kissed me at the gauge-house door. He tasted of sulphur. Everybody did.
For nine days it held. The needles sat high and steady and the Synod's men wrote it down. On the tenth day the fires in the drill-houses went cold.

Not out. Cold. You have not seen it, down here by your sea. A furnace burning white, and frost on the iron round it. Men pulled their hands off the rails with the skin left behind, and it was the frost that burned them. We have had the Cold Burn on the upper tiers since the Screaming Year. We had never had it at the Margin. The Margin was the hottest place in the world.
Let the hammer come round.

Then the whistle. The old women have a name for it. F-sharp. It is the heat remembering what it is for. It goes up out of the ground like a kettle the size of a mountain, and when you hear it you have four seconds, and the only thing in the world that will stand four seconds of it is basalt.
I was in the gauge-house. I did not decide anything. My body got down behind the wall before I knew the sound had a name.
One.
Two. I heard Odo shout my name from the number-six head. He was forty yards off in the open. He was not shouting for help. He was shouting to tell me where he was, so I would not come out to look.
Three. I did not come out. I want that printed. I did not go out. A Cinderholder will call that cold. Let them.
Four.

When I stood up, the frost had gone off everything at once and the air was so hot it hurt the eyes, and the Margin was quiet, and there was nobody on it. Not bodies. Shapes on the ground like the outlines a soot-fall leaves round a cart when you move it. Nine hundred of us, from the drill-heads out to the pipe-road. Seven came out alive. Six were in the gauge-houses, like me. The seventh is a scrapper of ours who dived behind a basalt wall-end out in the open, and he has not stopped talking about it since, loud, in every tavern on the tier, because when he stops he hears it.

The Consortium sent a clerk the next week with a form for the widows. Next of kin, number of the head, hours worked. There was a line for cause, and the cause was printed already. Seal failure. Nobody had looked at a seal.

They say in the deep galleries that the glass down there whispers. I never worked the deep galleries. But I will tell you what the Margin said, in the half-second before the whistle, under it, and I have not told this at home because I know what they would call me. It said a word. It sounded like a word. It sounded like somebody who has been holding something hot for a very long time, saying, enough.
They are talking about a strike in the guild-halls now. They talk about it between the falls, very low. When it comes, I will be there.
Odo kept his hand on it. On the ingot. Let the hammer come round.
notes: Suggested library: the Bonded Store at Stillwater. Sources: Vol II Realm III (the Thermal Margin, a ring of geothermal drills outside the caldera where the Synod increased bore-pressure and Tier Three's nine hundred died in four seconds; the F-sharp whistle, "thermal law re-asserting, four seconds to basalt"; eleven basalt tiers; soot-fall like grey snow; the Great Beat, stopped twice in two hundred years; the four-beat pulse people time their speech to; dialect "Still standing", "On the ingot", "cold" for cowardly, "He kept his hand on it"; Scrapper Muty of Tier Three, who lost his crew in 417 and survived by diving behind basalt and talks about it constantly, here unnamed); Series Bible Part VI (the Cold Burn: fire that freezes and frost that scalds; the ember-blind; the Deep Guilds hear the deep seams whisper) and Part VII (the Deep Guilds worked to death by the Consortium; the Gasket Strike brewing); Vol II Realm VI and Vol IV (Broadsheet Row, the free press of Port Cantabile); Vol II Realm I (broadsheets come into the Reach at Stillwater Landing); Review of the Cantabile serial (the Great Beat's four counts as Cinderhold's answer to the Narrow; no real Furnace House is blamed). The year 417 for the Margin is inferred from Muty's lost crew and is the one date here canon does not state outright. [PROPOSED]: Gerda Stahl, her husband Odo and her crew-mates; the shift-bell and the gauge-house; the Synod's pressure order arriving by runner; the printer's note.

title: What Is Written: A Short Account of the Silent Veil, for Novices
author: Umber, scribe of the House
origin: the House of the Silent Veil, the Spectral Woods
summary: An elderly Veil scribe welcomes new novices to the House with a short, proud history of her order, its rules and customs, and its happy arrangement with the Office of the Catalogue.
text: You have come up the long path through the willows, and stood under the round arch, and read the words over it, though you could not read them, because they are written in the old pitched hand. Here is what they say. What is written is not lost.
That is the whole of our faith, if we have one. The rest of this little book is only the furniture.

The House has stood on its rise above the pool for eleven hundred years. The Veil is older than the House. Nobody knows how much older, which is a strange thing to admit in a house of records, and I admit it. The order kept its books in other places before this one. They were burned, or drowned, or forgotten, which is how we learned to bind the Ledgers as we do. The first of them was bound eleven hundred years ago out of something that is not paper, and what it holds it holds against fire and water and time. You will not touch one for some years. When you do, you will feel why.
There are three rules, and you will learn them before you learn your letters. Write what happened. Write who it happened to. Do not comfort yourself in the margin.

The third is the hard one. You will be asked, in your life, to stand in a place where something terrible is happening and write it down while it happens. That is what the Veil is for. Kings have been crowned and realms have ended and cities have gone under the water, and in every one of those places there was a scribe of the Veil standing a little way off with a board on her arm, writing. We do not help. We do not hinder. We take no side, because a record that takes a side can be unwritten by the other one. This will seem cruel to you at first. It is the opposite of cruel. It is the one kindness that lasts. A thing that has been witnessed truly cannot be made never to have happened, by anyone, ever.

When you are sworn you will set your own name aside, as you set your cloak on the peg at the door, and take a designation from the ink-cupboard, as every scribe of the House has done. Mine is Umber. I have had it fifty-one years and I do not miss the other. It is kept. Nothing here is lost.

The House. The scriptorium is on the first floor at the east end: fourteen sloped desks in two rows, a stove at either end. The duty-scribe lights the east stove at the second bell. On the last day of every month we clean the desks with vinegar, so the whole floor smells of it, and of tallow, and of wet wool, because the Woods are damp and so are we. You will love that smell before your first winter is out, and you will never be able to describe it to anybody, so do not try.

Below the kitchens a stair goes down into the labyrinth. Its passages were cut to the shape of a chord that silences, so that nothing below can be heard above. Below the labyrinth are the stacks, where the roots of the Weeping Canopy come down through the ceiling. Novices are not taken there. On Memoryday the duty-scribe goes down with a lamp and reads one page of the dead aloud, in the flat voice, from wherever the last scribe left off, and comes up again. Nobody has ever been able to tell me to whom she reads it. It has been done every Memoryday for longer than the House has stood, and it will be done every Memoryday after I am gone.

The dead of the Woods are not like the dead of other places. When a soul goes out here the Echo catches it, as the songs say, and the Grove keeps it. So we keep the Canopy, the remembering of the dead, with more feeling than they do elsewhere, and on the night the Grove's water is highest we set lanterns on it, one name to a lantern, read aloud by whoever sets it. You will set your first lantern this year. Choose your name carefully.

The Office. A hundred and ten years ago the Veil came into the Synod's house as the Office of the Catalogue. Some of the old scribes wept, I am told, and three walked out into the Woods and were not seen again. I understand them, and I think they were wrong. Before the Office we were three hundred and twelve scribes with a leaking roof, begging vellum from the Moot. Now we have wages, and grey ink by the cask, and a place in the Organum's great archive where our oldest books are drier than they have ever been. The Office has never once asked us to alter an entry. The Registrar rules a page more beautifully than anyone I have known, and he likes to say that every name is a unit, by which he means that none may be counted twice and none left out. That is the Veil's own rule in a clerk's coat, and I was glad to hear it.

This year the Office has asked the House for twelve scribes for a great register of the Woods: every soul in the Grove and the villages round it, by name and voice and age, the most complete account of any country that has ever been attempted. I have put my own name forward, old as I am. I hope you will one day be chosen for such work yourselves.
It is a great thing to be trusted with every name in a country. I do not think a scribe of the Veil has ever been trusted with more.
notes: Suggested library: the Veil's scriptorium in the Mausoleum. Sources: Series Bible Part V (the Long Octave, when the Silent Veil kept the records; c. 300 SR the Veil absorbed as the Office of the Catalogue; Sable's name "only a Veil designation") and Part VII (the Office, "Every name is a unit", its Registrar); Vol I §5.3 (archivists sworn to record the death of civilizations and never intervene); Book One ch. 14 (the Veil's three rules; the Bound Ledger first bound eleven hundred years ago out of something that is not paper, holding against fire and water; reading flat and clear "in the voice of a person reading a will"), ch. 14 and 22 (the scriptorium: cold stone, tallow, wet wool, vinegar on the last day of every month, fourteen desks); Vol V §3 (the House, the scribes' own name for what the Synod's survey calls the Mausoleum of Chords; eleven hundred years; the motto over the round arch in pitched notation, What is written is not lost; the scriptorium on the first floor at the east end with sloped desks and a stove at each end, the east stove lit by the duty-scribe at the second bell; the labyrinth cut to the pattern of a silencing chord so nothing below can be heard above; the stacks under the Weeping Canopy's roots); Tobin's Journal p. 8 (the Echo that used to catch the Grove's dead, "in all the songs"); Vol VII §4 (Canopy, the remembering of the dead, still kept in 410); Vol VII (b) §4 (the Drowned Lanterns). Written in 410, before the Silencing of 416: the author does not know what the Office will do, and believes its great register of the Woods is a census. Nothing here says otherwise. [PROPOSED]: Umber as author; scribes' designations taken from the names of inks and pigments; the duty-scribe reading a page of the dead aloud on Memoryday (built on Vol VI §0.1, not explained); the Office's wages, grey ink and request for twelve scribes; the count of three hundred and twelve scribes before the absorption.

title: Going Up: How the Free Captains Took to the Air
author: Piet Ollander, keeper of the mast-tower, Port Cantabile
origin: printed on Broadsheet Row, Port Cantabile
summary: The old keeper of Port Cantabile's mast-tower explains, with no great respect for anybody, how skyships came to be, and why sea-captains who swore they never would have started to fly them.
text: I have kept the mast-tower at the end of the Long Mole for twenty-two years. It is sixty feet of iron rungs with a cradle at the top, and in the first ten of those years I moored perhaps one ship a month, and every one of them flew green and black and paid me in Consortium paper and looked at me as if I were part of the iron. Now I moor four a day, and half of them are ours, and they look at me as if I were their mother. I liked it better before. Here is how it changed.

Skyships are not ours. I say that first, because the young ones forget it. They were the Consortium's, and before that they were nobody's, because a Fortis-cut core will make a hull light but will not make her rise, and there was no drift-glass to be had. My father's generation never saw one. Then the drills got good. When the runic bore came in, the Consortium began to bleed the Velocity country, and what came out was a green glass, pale as sea-ice, that wanted more than anything in the world to move. Pack it in brass with a reed-valve on the end and it will strain at the valve like a dog at a door. The whole art of the skyship, the engineers say, is to persuade it that the direction it most wants to go is up. They say this as if it were a small thing. I have seen what it does when it changes its mind.

So the first skyships were survey craft, and then freighters, slow and fat under their envelopes, carrying for the Consortium what the Consortium did not trust to a road. A six-day march became a day's flight. The Synod built its own cutters and painted them iron-grey. The Coast watched them go over and spat, and went on sailing, because a Free Captain has a deck and a keel and the sea, and the sea has always been enough trouble for anyone.
Then the Screaming Year, and the sea changed its mind too.

You will have heard. The tides started singing in keys nobody could read. The water would forget, for an hour, that it was water, and go to a blue jelly round a hull, and when it remembered, the hull would be gone. And the trenches: a mouth in the sea, opening under a ship with no warning, with no bottom to it, and closing again on the far side. A captain who had sailed forty years could not tell you on any given morning whether the channel would still be a channel by noon. Hulls began to be laid up at their moorings. Crews went to the bottle-trade, or the drink, or both.

The first of ours to go up was Ysmay Cordell. She bought a condemned Consortium freighter at the yard auction for the price of its brass, patched the envelope with her own mainsails, and took four lift-tanks off a Synod cutter that had come down on the Cay, which is another story and a better one. She named her the Gull's Errand and brought her into my cradle on a still evening with half the Coast on the Mole to watch her fall in the harbour. She did not fall. She moored like a feather, came down my rungs, and said, I am not going back down there, and pointed at the water.

Then came the question of the Articles. The Articles were written for the sea, and the Free Captains will not have a thing they do not have an Article for. Was a ship in the air at sea? If she came over the harbour with nobody at the wheel, did the Ninth give her to the Harbour, as it would a hull drifting in under no hand? If she dropped a crate in the water, did the Sixteenth give it to whoever fished it up? The captains argued it three nights running. The Harbour ruled, in the flat voice it uses for hangings and tide-tables, that anything over the harbour is at sea, however high it goes. There is a rope from my cradle to the Mole-head derrick now, and on the derrick a board, and on the board the Articles, and somebody has chalked under them: and above.

Most of the Coast still sails. The old ones will not fly; they say a ship ought to have something under her she can feel. The young ones will not sail; they have seen too many laid-up hulls. And there is a third sort, which I have moored more than once, who fly and will not even look at the water. They come down my rungs with their eyes on the iron, and walk the whole length of the Mole looking at the town, and if you ask them about the sea they talk about the price of drift-glass, which is a scandal, a hundred and ten sovereigns a tank and rising.

People ask me if the air is safer. It is not. A holed tank does not burst. It weeps, a cobalt smoke, very slowly, and takes the lift out with it, and you have as long as it takes to weep to find somewhere to come down. I have watched ships come in nose-high and crabbing and nobody speaking on deck.

But I will tell you what the captains tell me, at the top of the tower, when they have had a drink. The sea wants you. That is what changed. It always had you, if it could get you, but now it wants you, the way a hound wants. The air does not want anything. It does not care whether you live. Some days, they say, that is a great comfort.
notes: Suggested library: the Bonded Store at Stillwater, or found aboard the Kestrel. Sources: Series Bible Part V (372 SR, the Carrow grandfather perfects the runic bore and siphoning becomes an industry; 398, the Valley of Velocity's law-collapse; 412, the Screaming Year), Part VI (the Drift: tides that sing, water that forgets its surface tension and becomes blue jelly, tonal trenches that open in the sea like mouths) and Part VII (the Free Captains under Oona Salt, Harbour-Queen; black glass and vox-bottles; mercenary and proud); Book One ch. 2 (Consortium freighters fly green and black, Synod cutters iron-grey; skyships with brass ribs, oak planking, patched envelopes and lift-tanks glowing the cobalt of drift-glass); ch. 21 (holed drift-glass does not explode, it weeps cobalt vapour); Book Two Part One (drift-glass is Velocity-glass tuned to lift, packed in brass with a reed-valve; the art is persuading it that the way it most wants to move is up; a tank is a hundred and ten sovereigns of drift-glass; the Articles of the Free Captains: the Ninth, a vessel under no hand belongs to the Harbour, and the Sixteenth, what lies below the tide-mark belongs to whoever brings it up, the Harbour taking a fifth); Vol IV Book Three (the mast-tower, sixty feet of iron rungs; the Long Mole; the derrick; Articles read aloud in a flat voice). Written in 416: the Wave-Cutter (dissolved 418) and the Kestrel's purchase (417) are after it, and no real captain is named. [PROPOSED]: Piet Ollander (renamed in review from Teodor Brisk, who is the Free Captain of lib_b_true_and_modest and the author of lib_c_saffery_lightfoot); Captain Ysmay Cordell, the first Free Captain to fly, and her ship the Gull's Errand; the Harbour's ruling that a ship aloft over the harbour is "at sea"; the first skyships as Consortium survey craft in the years after the runic bore; the saying "the sea wants you, the air does not care". Owner ruling (Oct 2026): a volume stands. Vol I §§ Fortis, Skyships: every skyship has a Fortis-cut lodestone core that cancels mass; the manuscript's drift-glass lift-tanks give the lift.
